Além das variáveis já citadas, a MGC também interfere na hemodinâmica de forma que a distribuição de gordura pode ditar o risco de doenças cardiovasculares.28 Dessa maneira, Han et al.,29 encontraram que em comparação com indivíduos normotensos, o percentual de gordura corporal foi significativamente maior no grupo de hipertensos.29 Park et al.,30 também demonstraram que indivíduos com alta porcentagem de gordura corporal foram associados ao aumento do risco de hipertensão mesmo com baixo IMC, CC ou relação cinturaquadril, sendo que o aumento do risco foi proporcional ao aumento do percentual.30 Nesse caso, através do aumento da MGC os níveis no plasma de biomarcadores inflamatórios como proteína C-reativa e interleucinas também podem aumentar, o que consequentemente, pode predispor o desenvolvimento de doenças cardiovasculares, incluindo a hipertensão.14 Como mencionado anteriormente, a distribuição de gordura pode ditar o risco de doenças cardiovasculares e, ainda nesse sentido, indivíduos com maior tecido adiposo visceral e depósitos de gordura ectópica tem uma prevalência ainda maior de distúrbios metabólicos como a Arq Bras Cardiol. 2023; 120(7):e20220728 Artigo Original Santos et al. Hipertensão Arterial e Fatores Associados hipertensão.31,32 Nas figuras 1 e 2 pode-se visualizar a área sobre a curva ROC para sensibilidade e especificidade para área de gordura visceral e glicemia plasmática em jejum encontradas no nosso estudo, as quais demonstram que ambas as variáveis obtiveram associações independentes com a HAS, destacando principalmente, a área de gordura visceral. O tecido adiposo visceral em excesso realiza a secreção de hormônios e moléculas que acentuam doenças cardiovasculares e também se torna resistente à insulina e leptina, podendo contribuir para resistência vascular e disfunção do sistema nervoso simpático.31 Já o tecido adiposo intra-abdominal em níveis elevados pode ser considerado como parte de fenótipo cujo resultado associa-se a uma alteração disfuncional do tecido adiposo subcutâneo e armazenamento ectópico de triglicerídeo, levando essa alteração morfológica a fazer parte de um conjunto de fatores de risco cardiometabólicos.33 Sabendo que a resistência à insulina pode contribuir para a resistência vascular e disfunção do sistema nervoso simpático,31 é importante destacar sua relação com os níveis de glicemia plasmática em jejum, visto que, à medida que a glicemia em jejum aumenta, o índice de sensibilidade a insulina diminui.34 Em um estudo realizado em japoneses foi observado que altos níveis de glicose em jejum foi independentemente e significativamente associado à hipertensão, sendo que a taxa de risco em participantes com glicemia acima ou igual a 7,0 mmol/l foi de 1,79 comparado com os participantes com glicemia menor que 5,6 mmol/l.15 Esses resultados corroboram com os nossos achados, já que a glicemia plasmática em jejum foi associada independentemente a HAS. As associações de glicemia plasmática em jejum e gordura visceral abdominal com a HAS descritos no presente estudo têm implicações práticas potenciais para intervenções de tratamento para melhorar os resultados em pacientes com obesidade e são provavelmente generalizáveis para populações em todo o mundo. No entanto, existem limitações para determinar se as associações estatísticas são causais e a direção das associações deve ser levada em consideração antes de se chegar a conclusões definitivas. Como o estudo é observacional, não é possível descartar os efeitos de confusão residual ou não mensurada como explicação para os resultados. Além disso, o desenho transversal não permite determinar se o quadro clínico de HAS precedeu ou foi influenciado pelo perfil metabólico e morfológico. É possível que as associações observadas da HAS com os marcadores bioquímicos e de composição corporal sejam bidirecionais. Conclusão Em conclusão, o presente estudo demonstra uma associação inversa e independente entre a concentração de glicose plasmática em jejum e a área de gordura visceral abdominal com HAS em pacientes obesos. Além disso, tanto a glicemia de jejum quanto a área de gordura visceral apresentaram alta sensibilidade para triagem de HAS. Os resultados chamam a atenção para a importância de intervenções para melhorar o controle de variáveis bioquímicas e de composição corporal, prevenir alterações na glicemia plasmática e atenuar o aumento da gordura visceral abdominal em pacientes com obesidade. BMC Oral Health Association between body roundness index and obstructive sleep apnea: a cross‑sectional study from the NHANES (2005–2008 to 2015– 2020) Ben Qin1,3, Miao Shu1,4, Song Cai1,3, YaShi Zhou1,3, JuKun Song2* and JuXiang Peng1,3*  Abstract  Background  Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is linked to obesity, and the body roundness index (BRI) is an innovative measure of obesity that more accurately reflects visceral and total body fat. The relationship between BRI and the likelihood of OSA is unclear, so we aimed to investigate the association between BRI and the prevalence of OSA. Methods  We used data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES; 2005–2008 to 2015– 2020) to conduct a cross-sectional study involving 24,476 individuals aged 18 years or older. OSA was assessed using three standardized NHANES questionnaire items measuring monthly daytime sleepiness, weekly apnea events, and habitual snoring frequency. A formula that uses the height and waist measures from the body measurements is used to calculate the BRI. Covariates, including sex, age, race/ethnicity, education level, marital status, povertyincome ratio (PIR), alcohol consumption, smoking status, high blood pressure (HBP), diabetes, and sleep duration were controlled using multivariate logistic regression models. Subgroup analyses, interaction tests, and smoothed curve fitting were also performed. Results  After controlling for confounders, BRI showed a positive correlation with OSA. Among the 24,476 participants aged 18 and older, 11,856 were diagnosed with OSA. The full model revealed a significant positive association between BRI and OSA incidence (OR = 1.11, 95% CI: 1.08–1.14, p < 0.0001). Participants in the highest percentile of BRI had an 87% greater likelihood of developing OSA compared to those in the lowest percentile (OR = 1.87, 95% CI: 1.62–2.16, p < 0.0001). Conclusion  BRI levels have shown a favorable correlation with the rising rates of OSA in the United States. The BRI serves as a straightforward anthropometric predictor of OSA. BMC Oral Health (2025) 25:666 Introduction The condition known as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) occurs when the airway in the upper respiratory tract repeatedly closes or becomes completely blocked while a person is sleeping. The main symptoms of OSA incorporate increased daytime sleepiness, apnea, awakenings, and snoring [1]. It raises the probability of accidents involving motor vehicles and workplaces [2], and in the United States, around 25% of adults are discovered to have obstructive sleep apnea [3]. From 1990 to 2010, the incidence of obstructive sleep apnea increased by approximately 30% [4]. The absolute increase for men was 7.5%, while the absolute increase for women was 4.2% [5]. Untreated obstructive sleep apnea can lead to several negative consequences, such as metabolic illnesses and cardiovascular diseases, posing a serious threat to public health [6]. Hypertension (HBP), dyslipidemia, obesity, cardiovascular disease, and other conditions are common settings in which OSA has been observed in prior research [7]. Among them, obesity is highly correlated with the prevalence of OSA [8]. Obese diabetics and people with severe obesity have an even higher prevalence of OSA, with estimates 50% and 60% of patients who are obese and have metabolic syndrome also have the condition [9]. Currently, the commonly used index for defining obesity is the Body Mass Index (BMI) (in kg/m2). The normal range is between 18.5–24.9, the overweight range is between 25–29.9, and a degree of obesity is 30 or higher [10]. However, body mass index (BMI) is not only not biologically reasonable, but it also fails to distinguish between central and peripheral fat locations and fails to suggest relevant phenotypes for research [11, 12]. Therefore, its limitations have led to doubts about its accuracy in assessing obesity [13]. Additionally, waist circumference (WC) is an indicator that can represent the relationship between fat distribution and central obesity, but it lacks consideration of a person’s height [14]. Body roundness index (BRI) was developed by Thomas et al. in 2013 and has the potential to forecast visceral fat percentage and quantity [15]. In contrast to conventional body measurements, BRI serves as a more accurate indicator of visceral fat and body fat percentage. There is substantial evidence indicating an association between obesity and OSA [16, 17]. Currently, there is still controversy regarding the research subjects on BRI and OSA. Research for this study was based on information culled from the NHANES database. This database has significant advantages. Firstly, it is non-institutionalized. The second advantage is the high sample size, which is indicative of a representative cross-section of the American population in terms of age, race, and other demographic variables. Consequently, our objective is to delve into the connection between BRI and OSA and discover its possible causes. Methods Study population The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) is the data source for this study, which surveys adults and children in the United States about their health and nutrition. Since 1999, the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) has been gathering data biennially. For information about the NHANES database, please visit https://​www.​cdc.​gov/​nchs/​nhanes/​index.​htm. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) is an annual survey that the CDC conducts to measure the general health and nutritional overall wellness of adults and children in the United States. The data used in this study originates from this survey. The uniqueness of this survey lies in its combination of interviews and physical examinations. Data spanning five cycles (2005–2008, 2015–2020) were analyzed, encompassing a total of 46,028 participants. From this initial pool, 8,001 individuals were excluded due to missing Body Roundness Index (BRI) data, and an additional 11,928 participants were excluded because of incomplete Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) data. After further excluding 1,623 individuals under the age of 18, the final study sample comprised 24,476 participants, all of whom were aged 18 years or older. Figure  1 shows the flow diagram for the population screening. Evaluation of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) According to previous reports, if participants respond "yes" to any of the three subsequent NHANES binary questions: it can be concluded that they have obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) [18]: (1) experiencing extreme daytime sleepiness 16–30 times a month despite sleeping for at least 7 h every night during the workday or on work evenings; (2) occasionally gasping, snorting, or ceasing to breathe; (3) occasionally snoring three times per week. Evaluation of the body roundness index (BRI) A novel metric for evaluating body shape, BRI takes two measurements: height in centimeters and waist circumference (WC) in centimeters. Height and WC data come from the participants’ body measurement data. To ensure accuracy, body measurement data is collected by trained health technicians from the mobile examination center. During the examination, a recorder aids the health technician. Before the measurement, the participants take off their shoes and garments. At one’s peak, one’s height is measured. Standing measurements of the region between the inferior rib and the superior aspect of the hip are Qin et al. BMC Oral Health (2025) 25:666 utilized to ascertain the waist circumference [19]. The BRI is computed using the formula: BRI = 364.2—365.5 * (1—[WC (cm) / 2π] 2 / [0.5 * height (cm)] 2) ½ [20]. Evaluation of covariates Age, gender, race/ethnicity (Mexican American, other Hispanic, non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, other race/ethnicity), education level (college or higher, high school, less than high school), marital status (widowed/separated/divorced, married/cohabiting, never married), and poverty-income ratio (PIR) are all factors that are taken into account based on clinical conditions and relevant studies [21]. Obesity is defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 40 kg/m or more, and there are four categories for BMI: less than 25.0, 25.0- < 30.0, 30.0- < 40.0, and over 40.0 [22, 23]. There are three groups based on smokers: those who have never smoked (< 100 smokes during their lifetime), those who have smoked in the past but have quit, and those who smoke now (smoking more than 100 smokes and still smoking) [24]. According to past research [25], the classification of alcohol drinkers is separated into four separate categories: never drinkers (having consumed < 12 drinks in a lifetime), moderate drinkers (men who have consumed 1 to 2 drinks per day in the past year and women who have consumed 1 drink per day in the past year), heavy drinkers (men who have consumed 3 to 4 drinks per day in the past year and women who have consumed 2 to 3 drinks per day in the past year), and binge drinkers (men who have consumed 5 or more drinks per day in the past year and women who have consumed 4 or more drinks per day in the past year). Sleep duration is categorized into insufficient (< 7  h per day), recommended sleep duration (7–9 h per day), and excessive amount of time spent sleeping (> 9  h per day) [26]. Hypertension (HBP) and diabetes were also included as covariates in the study. According to recent research [27], HBP is determined either by blood pressure measurements (≥ 130  mmHg systolic or ≥ 80  mmHg diastolic) taken by NHANES or by self-reporting of participants diagnosed by healthcare professionals. The history of diabetes was determined through self-reporting by participants, either diagnosed by healthcare professionals or identified through the review of prescriptions for diabetes treatment. Statistical analysis The study’s analysis utilized R (version 4.4.3) and EmpowerStats (2.0) application (http://​www.​empow​ersta​ts.​com) for statistical evaluation, considering the intricate multistage entire cohort survey. In three separate models, we investigated the link between BRI and OSA utilizing multivariate logistic regression: Model 1 lacked covariate adjustment, Model 2 compensated for age, sex, and race/ ethnicity, whereas Model 3 incorporated adjustments for all factors. We additionally evaluated the heterogeneity between BRI and obstructive sleep apnea by subgroup analyses, encompassing the following variables: sex, age, education level, body mass index (BMI), smokers, alcohol drinkers, hypertension (HBP), and sleep duration. In addition, regarding the handling of missing data, we employed the Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) method and repeated the primary analyses. Results Baseline characteristics of participants Table  1 displays the baseline characteristics of 24,476 individuals, including 11,856 patients with OSA and 12,620 patients without OSA. We used OSA as a column stratification variable, and there were significant differences in gender, age, race/ethnicity, education level, marital status, poverty-income ratio (PIR), smokers, alcohol drinkers, BMI, hypertension (HBP), diabetes, and sleep duration between the OSA group and the nonOSA group. Table  1 shows that OSA is more common in males, non-Hispanic whites, those with bachelor’s degrees or above, married or cohabitating, not smokers, moderate drinkers, those with high blood pressure, and those who get seven to nine hours of sleep per night without smoking. Association between BRI and OSA There is a link between BRI and the occurrence of OSA, as seen in Table  2. A higher prevalence of OSA was linked to a higher BRI in the unadjusted model (Model 1) (OR = 1.21, 95% CI = 1.20–1.23, p < 0.0001). When age, sex, and race were taken into account, this significance remained in Model 2 (OR = 1.23, 95% CI = 1.21–1.24, p < 0.0001). Lastly, a positive link between BRI and OSA persisted in Model 3, which further adjusted for education level, marital status, PIR, smokers, alcohol drinkers, BMI, HBP, diabetes, and sleep duration (OR = 1.11, 95% CI = 1.08–1.14, p < 0.0001). In the second quartile (OR = 1.43, 95% CI = 1.31–1.57, p < 0.0001), third quartile (OR = 1.66, 95% CI = 1.48–1.87, p < 0.0001), and fourth quartile (OR = 1.87, 95% CI = 1.62–2.16, p < 0.0001), OSA prevalence was higher than in the lowest quartile of BRI. Higher BRI was associated with an increase in the OR for OSA in each model (p for trend < 0.05). Utilization of smoothed curve fitting to look into the link between BRI and OSA. To gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between BRI and OSA, we employed smooth curve fitting techniques. The analysis revealed a positive correlation between BRI and OSA (Fig. 2). To further investigate this relationship, we performed threshold effect analysis, which identified an inflection point at a BRI value of 4.72. The likelihood ratio test showed a p-value less than 0.05, indicating statistical significance. Below the threshold of 4.72, each unit increase in BRI was associated with a 33% increase in the risk of OSA (OR = 1.33, 95% CI: 1.26– 1.40). Above this threshold, each unit increase in BRI corresponded to a 6% increase in OSA risk (OR = 1.06, 95% CI: 1.03–1.09) (Table 3). Subgroup analysis In order to investigate the potential correlation between BRI and OSA, a subgroup analysis was conducted. The analysis involved categorizing individuals based on parameters such as gender, age, education level, BMI, smoking status, drinking status, HBP, and sleep duration. The research results indicate that there is a consistent positive correlation between BRI and the prevalence of OSA in different groups. This positive correlation persists across all relevant subgroups, except for the BMI ≧ 40 kg/ m2 subgroup and the alcohol consumption status group, where the P values are all < 0.05, indicating good intergroup stability (Fig. 3). Comparison of BRI and BMI in predicting OSA The results of the ROC curves are shown in Table  4; Fig. 4. Although BMI demonstrated slightly greater discriminatory power (AUC: 0.637 vs. 0.633), BRI exhibited significantly higher specificity (0.698 vs. 0.648), corresponding to a 7.7% improvement in accurately excluding non-OSA subjects. Notably, this superior specificity was attained at a substantially lower cutoff value (4.6285 vs. 27.445 kg/m2), indicating BRI’s capacity for earlier OSA risk detection. Discussion The link between BRI and OSA is examined in this cross-sectional study that makes use of NHANES data. Our study found a positive correlation between BRI and an increased risk of OSA. This connection was still significant after controlling for all other factors. Even when looking at subgroups, this favorable correlation remains. Using smooth curve fitting, we find that BRI is positively correlated with OSA risk. The risk of OSA increases by 33% for each unit increase in BRI when BRI is less than 4.72; the risk increases by 6% for every unit increment in BRI when BRI is greater than 4.72. Obesity is recognized as an important risk indicator for the onset of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), with numerous epidemiological research demonstrating its correlation with OSA [28, 29]. Although there are many signs of obesity, the most popular one in recent years has been body mass index (BMI), which measures obesity generally. Numerous studies have demonstrated a favorable correlation between BMI and the risk of OSA [30, 31]. Park et  al. proposed the waist circumference index adjusted for weight (WWI) as a measure of obesity, which is also a commonly used index for assessing obesity. Compared to BMI, WWI is more reasonable and easier to assess obesity [32]. Similarly, cross-sectional studies have found that higher WWI values are positively correlated with the prevalence of OSA [33]. Additionally, other often utilized obesity metrics encompass Qin et al. Nonetheless, these conventional obesity measurement criteria possess drawbacks. As an example, body mass index (BMI) does not differentiate between visceral and subcutaneous fats, and waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) and waist circumference (WC) do not either. Body roundness index (BRI) testing uses waist circumference (WC) and height to determine percentage of body fat. Numerous studies have demonstrated that the BRI value can reliably forecast body fat and visceral fat tissue percentages [34–36]. Additionally, BRI is used to assess insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and hyperuricemia as a prognostic marker [37, 38]. In accordance with prior research, we determined that the BRI  serves as a predictive indicator for evaluating OSA, and it demonstrates superior predictive potential compared to the conventional BMI [39]. Our findings show that BRI exhibits significantly higher specificity than BMI in predicting OSA. In clinical settings requiring high diagnostic precision, this 7.7% relative improvement in specificity effectively counterbalances BRI’s 6.0% lower sensitivity (55.8% vs 49.8%), particularly valuable for ruling out non-OSA cases. However, in order to support our viewpoint, more comprehensive prospective cohort studies are needed. Obesity increases the risk of OSA through various pathophysiological processes. First, cardiovascular risk surrogate markers in obese patients (including endothelial impairment, systemic inflammation, and sympathetic nervous system activation) are significantly increased, thereby increasing the incidence of OSA [40]. Secondly, data from animal models indicate that OSA makes tissuelevel hypoxia worse [41]. The intensification of hypoxia in adipose tissue may represent a significant mechanism of cardiac metabolic dysfunction in OSA, as it is a major trigger for lipolysis, chronic inflammation, macrophage infiltration, reduced adiponectin levels, increased leptin levels, adipocyte death, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction [42], thereby increasing the risk of OSA. At the same time, obesity and weight gain are involved in an adverse positive feedback loop with the incidence and severity of OSA; weight gain increases the risk of OSA, and OSA leads to further weight gain [43]. Additionally, we analyzed the potential underlying causes of the BRI inflection point. BRI is calculated using a two-piece linear regression model, with the inflection point determined through a recursive method. Although BRI values cannot be directly converted into specific visceral fat percentages, the BRI score ranges from 1 to 16, with most individuals scoring between 1 and 10 [15]. Similarly, evidence suggests that exceeding a critical threshold of fat accumulation (beyond the inflection point) reduces compensatory responses, as observed in obesity-related bone metabolism disruptions [45]. This two-phase process—beginning with compensation and ending in decompensation—likely explains the underlying mechanism of the inflection point. Additionally, a 2020 review has reported that high BRI was associated with an increased risk of metabolic syndrome and various other diseases [34]. In our application using the NHANES database, the BRI inflection point of 4.72 may represent the threshold at which fat accumulation transitions from the compensatory phase to the decompensatory phase. When BRI exceeds 4.72, visceral fat accumulation may reach a critical threshold, leading to the failure of metabolic compensatory mechanisms, increased release of inflammatory factors, and a consequent significant elevation in disease risk, thus representing a clinically relevant risk level. Our research has several strengths. The study sample, sourced from NHANES, provides a large and reliable dataset. We also controlled for various confounding variables and performed subgroup analyses to ensure the applicability of our findings to a broader population. This study introduces a new body measurement, the Body Roundness Index (BRI), to explore the connection between obesity and OSA, and it is the first to examine the relationship between BRI and OSA. However, there are some limitations. First, the cross-sectional design inherently precludes causal inference between BRI and OSA, as temporal relationships cannot be established. This fundamental limitation underscores the need for longitudinal studies with repeated measures to elucidate potential cause-effect relationships. Second, the diagnosis of OSA in the NHANES database was solely based on questionnaires, which may introduce recall bias and potential misclassification. Additionally, the lack of objective measurements, such as polysomnography (PSG), represents a significant limitation. Although this approach has been used in previous studies, we recognize that the absence of objective measures may affect the accuracy of the diagnosis. Third, although we adjusted for key covariates, residual confounding may persist due to unmeasured factors such as physical activity, dietary habits, and medication use (e.g., sedatives), all known to modulate OSA risk. Fourth, we did not account for the effects of substance use or hormonal levels. Fifth, the non-significant associations observed in subgroups with BMI ≥ 40 kg/m2 and among alcohol consumers may reflect insufficient statistical power or unaccounted effect modifiers. These limitations warrant cautious interpretation of our findings, and future research should aim to address these gaps. Conclusion Our data shows that the prevalence of OSA is positively linked with BRI in adults in the US. As a straightforward anthropometric assessment, BRI can be used to forecast OSA. The possible processes and advantages of regulating BRI in OSA patients require additional research. Early prediction of OSA usually leads to better treatment outcomes, and this study aims to employ novel metabolic markers, visceral adiposity index (VAI), and lipid accumulation product (LAP) to evaluate the relationship to OSA. Methods  The data used in the current cross-sectional investigation are from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), which was carried out between 2015 and 2018. To examine the correlation between LAP and VAI levels and OSA, multivariate logistic regression analysis was adopted. In addition, various analytical methods were applied, including subgroup analysis, smooth curve fitting, and threshold effect analysis. Results  Among totally 3932 participants, 1934 were included in the OSA group. The median (Q1-Q3) values of LAP and VAI for the participants were 40.25 (21.51–68.26) and 1.27 (0.75–2.21), respectively. Logistic regression studies indicated a positive correlation between LAP, VAI, and OSA risk after adjusting for potential confounding variables. Subgroup analysis revealed a stronger correlation between LAP, VAI levels, and OSA among individuals aged < 60 years. Through smooth curve fitting, specific saturation effects of LAP, VAI, and BMD were identified, with inflection points at 65.684 and 0.428, respectively. Conclusion  This study demonstrates that elevated levels of LAP and VAI increase the risk of OSA, suggesting their potential as predictive markers for OSA and advocating for dietary and exercise interventions to mitigate OSA risk in individuals with high LAP and VAI levels. Lipids in Health and Disease (2024) 23:100 Introduction The hallmark of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is the partial or total collapse of the upper airway for at least ten seconds while you are asleep, resulting in reduced airflow (hypoventilation) or complete cessation (apnea). Its primary symptom is excessive daytime drowsiness [1, 2]. Based on epidemiological studies, OSA influ­ ences approximately 17% of women and 34% of men aged between 30 and 70 in the United States [3]. Left untreated, OSA can lead to severe health complications, including hypertension [4], cardiovascular diseases [5], and diabetes [6]. Therefore, it is crucial to find new and more accurate biomarkers for the early diagnosis of OSA is crucial. Recently, OSA has been regarded to be one of the seri­ ous complications caused by obesity [7]. Obesity is char­ acterized by the accumulation of visceral fat. However, conventional measures, including BMI, can only roughly assess obesity status and cannot differentiate between subcutaneous and visceral fat. As a novel anthropometric index, the visceral adiposity index (VAI) has been shown to be effective in evaluating adult visceral fat distribution and dysfunction. Waist circumference (WC) and body mass index(BMI) can be applied to compute VAI, which can additionally evaluate triglyceride (TG) and high-den­ sity lipoprotein (HDL) [8]. Clinical studies have shown that VAI can effectively identify individuals at higher risk of metabolic disorders associated with visceral obe­ sity, including insulin resistance, lipid abnormalities, and cardiovascular risk factors [9–11]. In addition, the lipid accumulation product (LAP) index, derived from the combination of waist circumference and TG, can also assess and show the status of abdominal lipid accumula­ tion. Its predictive efficacy is superior to traditional indi­ cators like BMI and waist-height ratio (WHtR) [12, 13], and it has also exhibited good predictive performance in some clinical conditions [14, 15]. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) is a meticulously designed large-scale clini­ cal registry database with complete follow-up, making it well-suited for discussing the relationship between VAI and LAP with OSA. Thus, this study is aimed at evaluat­ ing the association between VAI and LAP for OSA, and we assume that VAI and LAP make a strong predictive effect on OSA. This study comprehensively evaluates OSA using VAI and LAP through effectively utilizing the powerful advantages of the NHANES database and expects the research results to provide guiding signifi­ cance for clinical practice. Methods Study population and research design NHANES, a nationally representative, stratified, mul­ tistage probability sample survey, is performed by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) [16]. Its aim is to evaluate the relationship between nutrition health promotion and illness prevention. This survey combines interviews with physical examinations and is performed in two-year cycles, covering demographic, dietary, examination, laboratory, and questionnaire sec­ tions. More information concerning the NHANES data­ base can be accessed at http://www.cdc.gov/nhanes. Between 2015 and 2018, totally 19,225 participants were involved. Based on strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, this study ultimately determined a sample size of 3932 U.S. adults from the NHANES 2005–2018 cycle. Specifically, this study excluded 6741 participants with missing OSA data, 7627 participants with missing VAI and LAP data, 439 individuals under 20 years of age, and 486 participants with missing covariate values (Fig. 1). Assessment of OSA In accordance with earlier studies, OSA is diagnosed when a person answers “yes” to at least one of the follow­ ing three NHANES questions [17]: (1) being excessively sleepy in the day even though they get at least 7 h of sleep per night, as reported 16–30 times; (2) experiencing epi­ sodes of gasping, snorting, or stopping their breath on three or more occasions per week; (3) snoring on three or more occasions every week. Assessment of LAP and VAI Based on previously established equations indicated by Kahn and Amato et al. [12, 18], LAP and VAI were cal­ culated according to gender using the following formu­ las, where TG and HDL are in mmol/L, WC is in cm, and BMI is in kg/m^2. Males : LAP = (WC −65) ∗TG Females : LAP = (WC −58) ∗TG Males : V AI = WC 39.68 + 1.88*BMI ∗ TG 1.03 ∗ 1.31 HDL Females : V AI = WC 36.58 + 1.89*BMI ∗ TG 0.81 ∗ 1.52 HDL Measurement of covariates Based on previous studies [19, 20], potential confound­ ing factors related to VAI, LAP, and OSA were included in the final analysis. Age, race, gender, educational attainment, marital status, and the income-to-poverty ratio (PIR) were among the demographic factors. Mexi­ can Americans, non-Hispanic whites, non-Hispanic blacks, other Hispanics, and other races were shown to be the different categories for race. Educational level was Zhou et al. Lipids in Health and Disease (2024) 23:100 divided into the following three types: below high school, high school or above, and above high school. Marital status was categorized into two types: “married or part­ nered” and “living alone”. BMI, calculated through divid­ ing weight (in kilograms) by height (in meters squared), was also regarded as an examination variable. Ques­ tionnaire surveys included alcohol consumption, smok­ ing status, and diabetes. Participants self-reported their medical history to assess chronic health conditions, indi­ cating whether a doctor or other health professional had informed them of specific health conditions. Participants’ smoking status was categorized in line with whether or not they had ever smoked 100 cigarettes or more. “Ever have 4/5 or more drinks every day” was the definition of alcohol consumption status. Statistical analysis VAI and LAP were divided into quartiles (Q1 to Q4) from lowest to highest. Categorical characteristics were reported as proportions, whereas continuous variables were summarized as means with standard errors (SE). Weighted Student’s t-tests or weighted chi-square tests were utilized to explore differences between individuals stratified by gender for continuous variables. For the purpose of exploring the odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) between OSA and LAP, VAI, multiple logistic regression models were adopted. Three models were applied: Model 1 (unadjusted), Model 2 (adjusted for age, gender, and race only), and Model 3 (fully adjusted for age, race, gender, educational level, income-to-poverty ratio, marital status, BMI, alcohol consumption, smoking status, and diabetes). Interaction and subgroup analyses were performed to explore poten­ tial modifications to this association by covariates. Additionally, smooth curve fitting based on generalized additive models (GAM) was used to evaluate the nonlin­ ear relationship between VAI, LAP, and OSA. P < 0.05 was applied as the statistical significance threshold. R (version 3.4.3) and EmpowerStats (version 2.0) were adopted for the statistical analysis. Results Baseline characteristics of participants Totally 3932 individuals met the study criteria and were involved in the analysis. Table  1 outlines the baseline characteristics of participants grouped by the pres­ ence or absence of OSA, with 1934 individuals being included in the OSA group. The mean age of partici­ pants was 50.21 ± 17.32 years, with females comprising 51.32% and males 48.68%. The Median (Q1-Q3) of LAP and VAI were 40.25 (21.51–68.26) and 1.27 (0.75–2.21), respectively. Participants in the OSA group had higher VAI and LAP values when compared with those in the non-OSA group, with statistical significance. In addition, significant differences were observed among all OSA patients in terms of age, gender, race, marital status, edu­ cational level, alcohol consumption history, and diabetes history (P < 0.05). Association between LAP, VAI, and OSA With the purpose of further investigating the correlation between OSA and LAP, VAI, three multiple regression models were constructed for analysis (Table  2). In the unadjusted Model 1, multiple logistic regression analysis suggested that there existed a significant positive corre­ lation between OSA and LAP, VAI. After the adjustment for all covariates in Model 3, the significant association between OSA and LAP, VAI persisted (OR = 1.002, 95% CI: 1.001, 1.004, P = 0.0069; OR = 1.042, 95% CI: 1.006, 1.080, P = 0.0219), suggesting that for every one-unit increase in LAP, VAI levels, the risk of OSA elevated by 0.2% and 4.2%, respectively. Subsequently, LAP and VAI were converted into categorical variables based on quar­ tiles for sensitivity analysis. In the fully adjusted Model 3, when comparison with the lowest quartile, participants in the highest LAP and VAI quartiles exhibited a signifi­ cantly increased risk of OSA by 45.5% and 29.5%, respec­ tively, with statistical significance (OR = 1.455, 95% CI: 1.142, 1.853, P = 0.0024; OR = 1.295, 95% CI: 1.060, 1.583, P = 0.0115). To further visualize the correlation between LAP, VAI, and OSA, smooth curve fitting based on Model 3 was conducted. Results in Fig.  2 indicated a nonlin­ ear relationship between LAP, VAI, and OSA. Then, threshold effect analysis was performed to clarify their relationship(Table  3). The inflection point for LAP was determined as 65.684 (log-likelihood ratio = 0.003), indi­ cating that when LAP levels were below 65.684, every one-unit increase in LAP showed a relationship to a 0.9% elevation in the risk of OSA. When LAP levels exceeded 65.684, the correlation between LAP and OSA risk disap­ peared, suggesting that further increases in LAP did not significantly elevate the risk of OSA. Similar results were observed for VAI with an inflection point at 0.428 (loglikelihood ratio = 0.008), suggesting different effects of VAI on OSA risk below and above this threshold. Subgroup analyses Multiple subgroup analyses and interaction tests based on various covariates were adopted for evaluating the robustness of the relationship between LAP, VAI, and OSA, and for identifying potential population differ­ ences (Table 4). The findings of subgroup analysis indi­ cated a consistent relationship between LAP, VAI, and OSA across most subgroups. Notably, a significant inter­ action was observed between LAP, VAI, and age (inter­ action P < 0.05). In participants who aged < 60 years, a strong and significant positive correlation was observed Zhou et al. Lipids in Health and Disease (2024) 23:100 (OR = 1.004, 95% CI: 1.002, 1.006, P = 0.00156; OR = 1.065, 95% CI: 1.020, 1.113, P = 0.0215), while this association became non-significant in participants aged ≥ 60 years. This suggests that higher levels of LAP and VAI may increase the likelihood of developing OSA in individuals aged < 60 years. Discussion In the present cross-sectional study involving 3932 rep­ resentative adults, this work discovered a significant positive correlation between VAI, LAP, and OSA. Impor­ tantly, non-linear relationships were observed between LAP, VAI, and OSA, with saturation values of LAP (65.684) and inflection points of VAI (0.428) identified for all participants. This suggests that there exists a strong correlation between LAP, VAI levels, and OSA within specific ranges, indicating the potential clinical significance of maintaining ideal LAP and VAI levels in lowering the risk of OSA. Obstructive sleep apnea and obesity exhibit a complex interdependence [21]. Obesity, especially excess abdomi­ nal fat, is a main risk factor for the development and exacerbation of OSA. The accumulation of fat around the neck and upper airway can result in airway narrowing or obstruction during sleep, causing episodes of complete or partial cessation of breathing (apneas or hypopneas) [22, 23]. Moreover, evidence suggests that OSA itself can change the lipid profile [31]; OSA itself exacerbates lipid abnormalities by increasing insulin resistance and inflammatory responses, creating a negative feedback loop [32, 33]. The elevation in blood lipids puts pressure on the cardiovascular system, elevat­ ing the workload of the heart and blood vessels, which is unfavorable for patients with OSA, as they are already under the cardiovascular burden caused by intermittent hypoxia. This bidirectional relationship between OSA and obesity creates a vicious cycle where one condition exacerbates the other. Both conditions share common risk factors, including a sedentary lifestyle, poor dietary habits, and genetic predisposition, which further compli­ cates their relationship [34]. Compared with traditional methods, which include computed tomography and magnetic resonance imag­ ing, VAI and LAP offer simple and non-invasive means to assess visceral fat accumulation. Introduced in 2010, VAI utilizes multiple metabolic markers to accurately assess visceral fat distribution and associated metabolic abnor­ malities. LAP, proposed in 2005, has been found to better predict cardiovascular diseases than traditional BMI [35, 36]. These indices provide additional tools for evaluating risk factors associated with obesity and metabolic abnor­ malities. A lot of studies have demonstrated the pre­ dictive capabilities of VAI and LAP in various diseases, including diabetes and cardiovascular diseases [37, 38]. This study reveals a positive association between VAI, LAP, and OSA, consistent with findings by Deng et al. Hence, both indices should be considered in clinical OSA management [21]. “Previous meta-analyses have also reported the similar findings [39], suggesting that lipid indexes, including LAP and VAI, possess commendable diagnostic capability ies. For the research findings, this study compared and discussed them with relevant litera­ ture. Firstly, both VAI and LAP have been found to pre­ dict cardiovascular diseases better when compared with individual lipid components and are both associated with OSA, a correlation the results also affirm. However, when comparing ROC curves, it could be found that the asso­ ciation between LAP and OSA is significantly stronger. LAP has also been identified as one of the best param­ eters for predicting hypertension, diabetes, and ischemic heart disease in OSA patients [40, 41]. In other studies, VAI has been identified as a marker for predicting insu­ lin resistance in OSA patients [42], potentially provid­ ing a powerful tool for identifying OSA patients at risk of MetS [43]. In other study, LAP and CMI (cardiometa­ bolic index) were shown to be related to OSA and MetS, but CMI has a more practical threshold in identifying disease states [44]. In the final study, LAP and the TyG index were indicated to be associated with an elevated risk of OSA and cardiometabolic diseases [45]. In sum­ mary, both VAI and LAP are related to OSA or cardio­ metabolic diseases, but results may vary among different studies, and this study also reports certain threshold values, although their optimal thresholds still need to be identified in large-scale follow-up studies. In subgroup analyses, this study has newly identified that higher lev­ els of LAP and VAI are more likely to increase the odds of developing OSA in individuals younger than 60 years, while this association appears to diminish in those aged 60 years and above. This may be caused by age-related changes in metabolism and physiology, including altera­ tions in lipid accumulation patterns and associated meta­ bolic indicators [46, 47]. Elderly individuals are more susceptible to hypertension, diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases, which may influence sleep quality or metabolic indicators, thus attenuating the association between LAP, VAI, and OSA. Interestingly, Hai Deng and colleagues have also provided an explanation for this phenom­ enon, suggesting that this difference can be clarified by the contradictory impact of adipose tissue distribution on older adults [21]. Furthermore, Auyeung TW and his colleagues conducted a five-year longitudinal study involving 4000 elderly individuals, finding that older men exhibit resistance to the harmful effects of overweight and obesity; mild overweight or obesity may even have a protective effect [48]. Study strengths and limitations This research has certain advantages. As a vital epide­ miological study in the United States, NHANES collects data with strict quality control procedures, and the con­ clusions drawn are quite reliable. The utilization of VAI and LAP enables a comprehensive evaluation of visceral fat distribution, devoid of the drawbacks of high costs, radiation exposure, and operational complexity associ­ ated with CT and MRI scans. As a result, this approach can be more widely used in clinical and screening set­ tings. Additionally, this study’s results provide certain guiding significance for clinical practice. Clinical staff can better identify individuals with high VAI and LAP for OSA screening, as they can serve as very efficient diag­ nostic biomarkers. At the same time, clinicians can also develop more personalized treatment plans for patients based on VAI and LAP. However, this study still has the following limitations: (1) The use of a cross-sectional design precludes the observation of dynamic changes in physical indicators. (2) Reliance on data from US adults may limit the gen­ eralizability to other populations. (3) Owing to the lack of polysomnography data collection in the NHANES process, OSA was determined based on NHANES ques­ tionnaire responses, which may introduce recall or selfreport bias. Conclusion In conclusion, this study utilizing NHANES data estab­ lishes a significant association between elevated LAP and VAI levels and the risk of OSA, suggesting their utility as predictive markers for OSA. Moderating LAP and VAI levels may not only delay OSA progression but also serve as preventive measures. Healthcare interventions focus­ ing on dietary and exercise modifications are recom­ mended for individuals with high LAP and VAI levels to mitigate OSA risk. The obtained findings underscore the importance of incorporating LAP and VAI assessments into clinical evaluations to guide targeted interventions and improve outcomes in individuals at risk of OSA. The current obesity assessment indicators have poor ability to distinguish between fat and muscle. Relative fat mass (RFM) a new indicator of obesity that takes into account gender differences and can predict body fat conditions has advantage in this respect. This study aimed to investigate the potential association between RFM and OSA, as well as the possible mediating effect of hypertension. Methods  This cross-sectional study used data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey conducted in 2005–2008 and 2015–2018. Multivariate logistic regression, restricted cubic splines (RCS), and subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the association between RFM and OSA. In addition, the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) of different obesity indicators was compared to assess their predictive ability for OSA. Mediation analysis was used to explore the potential mediating role of hypertension in the positive correlation. Results  The study included 13,532 participants with complete study data, of which 6854 were assessed as having OSA according to the criteria, accounting for 50.65% of the study population. The results of the multivariate logistic regression model with fully adjusted covariates showed that the odds ratio of RFM was 1.096 (95%CI:1.084–1.109, P < 0.001). The results of the RCS show that RFM is nonlinearly correlated with OSA (P for nonlinear < 0.01). Subgroup analysis showed that the association between RFM and OSA was stronger in female and people younger than 60. The ROC also indicates that, compared with the body roundness index and weight-adjusted-waist index, RFM showed potential as a predictor. Mediation analysis and sensitivity analysis showed that hypertension had a statistically significant but poorly robust mediating effect between RFM and OSA. Conclusion  There is a positive and nonlinear correlation between RFM and OSA. Hypertension plays a potential mediating role in the positive association between RFM and OSA, but its robustness is poor. Nutrition Journal (2025) 24:141 Introduction Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) refers to recurrent epi­ sodes of partial or complete collapse of the upper air­ way during sleep, resulting in a respiratory event such as hypopnea or apnea lasting at least 10  s [1]. OSA may affect normal life, such as daytime sleepiness [2], decreased quality of life [3], and increased motor vehi­ cle accidents [4, 5]. OSA has been proven to be associ­ ated with a variety of diseases, including cardiovascular disease [6–8], adverse pregnancy outcomes [9], diabetes mellitus [10], cognitive impairment [11], and cancer [12]. OSA occurs in people of all ages and genders, but there are significant gender differences in the prevalence of OSA. A community-based study in the United States showed that among adults aged 30–70, about 34% of men and 17% of women have OSA, and about 13% of men and 6% of women have moderate or severe OSA [13]. Young also mentioned in the article that by summarizing the results of several OSA studies, about 3–28% of the popu­ lation suffers from mild OSA, and about 1–14% suffers from severe OSA [14]. In addition, OSA is more common in the elderly population. A study of the elderly showed that 70% of males and 56% of females aged 65–95 had OSA [15]. A community study of children in China also showed that the prevalence of OSA in children was 5.8% in boys and 3.8% in girls according to the second edition of the International Criteria for Sleep Disorders [16]. At present, studies have confirmed the association between obesity and OSA [17, 18], and existing literature has shown that obesity types grouped according to BMI are related to the severity of OSA [19]. However, the cur­ rent obesity index BMI, has poor ability to distinguish fat distribution [20], and it was found in the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey in the United States that the accuracy of BMI in distinguishing obesity in men and women was 82% and 94%, respectively [21]. Based on this situation, many indicators with better abil­ ity to distinguish fat distribution than BMI have emerged, and it has been shown that OSA is associated with obe­ sity assessed by BRI (body roundness index) and WWI (weight-adjusted-waist index) [22, 23]. As a new, simple, and low-cost index, RFM (relative fat mass) can accu­ rately diagnose obesity. It was designed by establishing a regression model for various anthropometric indica­ tors to analyze their correlation with body fat percentage. Finally, height and waist circumference indicators with the highest correlation were selected to establish a calcu­ lation formula, taking the difference in body fat between genders into account. Two formulas were designed for men and women, and the overall ability to predict body fat was greater than BMI [24]. RFM has been widely used as a new indicator to assess obesity, and RFM is associ­ ated with depression [25], periodontitis [26], stroke [27], gallstones [28], female infertility [29], type 2 diabetes [30], and cardiovascular mortality [31]. Hypertension is a disease associated with both obesity and OSA. Obesity and excessive body fat can increase the risk of hypertension [32–34]. As an index to predict body fat, RFM has also been confirmed to be positively correlated with hypertension [35]. Similarly, OSA has been confirmed to have a two-way effect with hyper­ tension [36], and OSA patients have a higher incidence of hypertension, and OSA is also one of the risk factors for hypertension [37]. However, the mediating effect of hypertension on OSA is still unclear. Because the relationship between RFM and OSA is not clear, our study aimed to demonstrate the association between RFM and OSA by examining the NHANES data from 2005 to 2008 and 2015 to 2018, and investigated the mediating role of hypertension as a mediator. Evaluating the ability and utility of RFM as a new predictor of OSA compared with other indicators of obesity, providing new ideas and valuable insights for the prevention and treat­ ment of OSA in the public health field. Methods Study participants All data used were published by the US National Cen­ ter for Health Statistics. Data were derived from the NHANES database, a series of nationally representa­ tive cohort surveys designed to monitor public health in the US population. Since 1999, the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey has been conducted in a two-year cycle, collecting data from home inter­ views and study visits at mobile test centers. The survey was approved by the National Ethics Review Board for Research in Health Statistics, and participants signed informed consent. Detailed NHANES research design and data are available at ​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​w​w​w​.​c​d​c​.​g​o​v​/​n​c​h​s​/​n​h​a​n​ e​s​/. Because data on the frequency of snoring during sleep and on the frequency of difficulty breathing, gasp­ ing, or stopping breathing during sleep were available in the NHNAES database only for the years 2005–2008 and 2015–2018, we included eight years of survey data from four NHANES cycles, 2005–2008 and 2015–2018. The study population consisted of nonpregnant adults 20 years or older and was complex weighted to be as a predictor of OSA, but more prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings and determine the causal relationship between RFM and OSA. Keywords  Relative fat mass, Obesity, Obstructive sleep apnea, Hypertension, NHANES Guo et al. To ensure the rigor and precision of the experiment, specific exclusion criteria were applied, excluding 18,038 par­ ticipants younger than 20 years of age and pregnant par­ ticipants, excluding 2248 participants with missing RFM data, excluding 70 participants with missing OSA-related data. 5834 participants with missing data on covariates, BRI, BMI, and WWI were excluded. The final analysis included 13,532 participants from the NHANES data­ base. (Fig. 1) Calculation of RFM and other measures to assess obesity We calculated stance height, weight, and waist circumfer­ ence from the physical examination data in the NHANES database with the following formula, in which measure­ ments were collected by trained health technicians at a mobile examination center (MEC). The body measure­ ment examination room for each MEC was identical in terms of layout and equipment. Planned device calibra­ tion was performed by health technicians and verified by supervisors. Calculation of RFM Woolcott et al. proposed the concept of relative fat mass (RFM) for the first time in 2018 [24] and defined the formula of relative fat mass for different genders. We put the waist circumference (cm) and standing height (cm) data of participants who met the research criteria into the formula for calculation. RFM (women) = 76 −(20 × height (cm) waist circumference (cm)) RFM (men) = 64 −(20 × height (cm) waist circumference (cm)) Calculation of BRI Thomas et al. proposed the model concept of ellipse for the first time in their 2013 article [38], and defined the formula of body roundness index (BRI). We put the waist circumference (cm) and standing height (cm) data of par­ ticipants who met the research criteria into the formula for calculation. Nutrition Journal (2025) 24:141 Calculation of BMI We calculated BMI by bringing height and weight data from participants who met the study criteria into the fol­ lowing formula. BMI = weight (kg) height (m)2 Calculation of WWI Weight-adjusted-waist index (WWI) was originally pro­ posed by Park et al. [39], An index that converts waist cir­ cumference into weight adjusted for waist circumference by least squares regression of waist circumference and weight. We took waist circumference and weight data from participants who met the study criteria into the fol­ lowing formula to calculate WWI. WWI = waist circumference (cm) √ weight (kg) Assessment of OSA In terms of the assessment of OSA, we borrowed from published articles [40] and evaluated according to the sleep module in the questionnaire data of the NHANES database. Participants were assessed for the pres­ ence of OSA when they met any of the following three conditions: (1) Participant’s sleep duration on weekdays and weekends was 7 h or more, and the number of times participants felt sleepy during the day in a month was 16–30. (2) Participants reported snoring frequency at sleep three or more times per week during the past 12 months. (3) Participants’ responses regarding the frequency of breathing difficulties, wheezing, or cessation of breathing during sleep in the past 12 months were three or more times per week, including wheezing, snoring, or cessation of breathing. Measurement of covariates Potential confounders associated with RFM and OSA were included in the analysis based on published studies. Covariates considered included demographic character­ istics: age, gender, race, education level, marital status, and poverty-to-income ratio (PIR). Related lifestyle hab­ its: smoking status, alcohol intake status, and physical activity levels. Relevant dietary status: total calorie intake and total fat intake. And whether there are certain dis­ eases or a family history: diabetes, hypertension, cancer, family history of diabetes, cardiovascular disease. For the convenience of subsequent analysis and discussion, age was set as a categorical variable (> = 60, < 60). Educational level groupings were defined as (less than high school, high school, more than high school); Marital status was categorized as (Married, Widowed, Divorced, Separated, Never married, and Living with partner.); Poverty to income ratio (PIR) was classified as (< 1.5,1.5–3.5,>3.5); Smoking status was classified into smoking group and non-smoking group according to whether they smoked 100 cigarettes in their lifetime. Alcohol intake was clas­ sified into drinking group and non-drinking group according to whether they consumed four or five or more alcoholic beverages per day. The level of physical activity was classified according to the physical activity involved in the job, including mild physical activity and less, mod­ erate physical activity, and heavy physical activity. Total energy and fat intake were expressed as the total energy and fat from a participant’s daily diet. Health status was classified according to whether they had been told by a doctor or health professional that they had diabetes, hypertension, or a family history of diabetes. Participants were classified as having cardiovascular disease (CVD) based on whether they suffered from congestive heart failure, coronary heart disease, angina pectoris, or heart attack. Statistical analysis Analyses were performed according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) NHANES Data analysis guidelines. Because eight years of data from four survey cycles were used, complex weighting was performed using quarter-weight (WTMEC2YR), stratification (SDMVSTRA), and main sampling unit (SDMVPSU). Continuous variables are presented as means with SD (standard deviation) and were compared between groups with the use of analysis of variance. Cat­ egorical variables were expressed as frequencies and per­ centages, and group comparisons were performed using the χ2 test for categorical variables. Multivariate Logistic regression was used to ana­ lyze the correlation between RFM and OSA in different models, and regression analysis was performed in the whole population, male population, and female popula­ tion, respectively. Three regression models were devel­ oped: Model 1: Unadjusted for confounders. Model 2: Demographic factors such as age (classification), gender(removed when studying male and female popu­ lations), race, marital status, educational level, and PIR were adjusted. Model 3: Based on Model 2, the drink­ ing status, smoking status, the level of physical activity, total energy intake, total fat intake, diabetes, hyperten­ sion, history of diabetes, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and cancer status were further adjusted. The Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT) based on Rao-Scott corrected F-test Guo et al. Nutrition Journal (2025) 24:141 was used to verify the effect of adding nonlinear terms on the model fit and to provide evidence for the use of restricted cubic spline (RCS), which was used to explore the dose-response relationship between RFM and OSA. We used the fully adjusted model to draw the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) of RFM and other obe­ sity indicators (BRI, BMI and WWI), and systematically compared the statistical differences in the area under the curve (AUC) among the curves of each indicator through the “DeLong” test method. To reduce the familywise error rate and to account for the association of the four measures of obesity, the Holm-Bonferroni correction method was used for multiple comparisons of DeLong’s suggested P values. The differential diagnostic efficacy of RFM for OSA was evaluated. Subgroup analyses and tests for interaction were performed for categorical covariates. To investigate the mediating role of hypertension between RFM and OSA, we performed mediation analy­ sis based on the R language “Mediation” package to show the indirect, direct, and overall effects of hypertension. “Mediation” is based on a quasi-Bayesian approach, and 1000 Monte Carlo simulations are run for mediation analysis. In order to verify the robustness of the model, a sensitivity analysis was performed using a multivariate regression model after grouping RFM into quintiles. The robustness of the mediation analysis was evaluated by the “Medsens” function and “E-value”. All statistical analyses were performed with the use of R, version 4.4.3 (http://www.R-project.org, R ​F​o​u​n​d​a​t​i​o​n​ )​. All statistical tests were two-sided, and significance was considered to be P < 0.05. Discussion This study aimed to examine the association between RFM and OSA using data from NHANES conducted between 2005 and 2008 and between 2015 and 2018, and to compare the association with other obesity measures. Our study mainly found a statistically significant positive relationship between RFM and OSA in the US popula­ tion. The results showed that individuals with high RFM had a higher incidence of OSA compared with those with low RFM. The research results were consistent in both the male and female populations, and the robustness of the results was demonstrated in gender stratification through a quintile approach (the sensitivity analysis sec­ tion in the supplementary materials). Through media­ tion analysis, we found that hypertension had a potential mediating role in the positive relationship between RFM and OSA. The association mechanism between RFM and OSA Although the pathological mechanism of RFM and OSA has not been fully elucidated, the following mechanis­ tic hypotheses are proposed based on the available evi­ dence. First of all, RFM is an index to predict body fat mass and evaluate obesity [24]. Therefore, the higher the RFM index, the higher the body fat mass and the more serious the obesity degree. Obesity has been confirmed to be the most important cause of OSA in many studies [17, 40–42]. The reason for this phenomenon may be the anatomical imbalance of the pharynx caused by obesity, which eventually leads to periodic obstruction of the pharyngeal airway [43]. Moreover, reduced vital capac­ ity [44] and weakened respiratory muscle function [45] caused by central obesity further promote pharyngeal obstruction [46], making obese people more prone to OSA. In addition, waist circumference is also an impor­ tant factor affecting OSA. Unal et al. ‘s study confirmed that people with a high waist circumference and waist to height ratio have a higher probability of OSA [47], and Yildirim’s study also showed that an increase in waist circumference will increase the risk of OSA regardless of obesity [44], which may be because waist circumfer­ ence reflects abdominal fat mass. Individuals with high abdominal fat mass may reflexively affect upper airway dimensions when supine [44], although this individual was not assessed as obese. RFM index uses waist circum­ ference and height as predictors of body fat [24], so it also has a good ability to distinguish the above conditions. The RFM index calculated by waist circumference can take into account the condition of abdominal fat. Advantages of RFM over other measures of obesity Our study did not find that the predictive ability of BRI for OSA was greater than BMI, as mentioned by Pan et al. [22], possibly due to the difference in the selection of covariates between RFM and BMI. However, the above results showed that RFM has a better predictive abil­ ity than WWI, and is better than BRI and BMI in some populations, under the same covariate adjustment model. In addition, Pan’s study showed that BRI was better than BMI and WWI in the prediction of OSA [22], while RFM had higher predictive ability than BRI in the whole popu­ lation and male population, which was enough to prove that RFM was a more effective predictor of OSA. Based on the existing research evidence, the validity of BMI as an obesity assessment tool has significant limi­ tations, especially in the identification of differences in body fat distribution [20]. In order to enhance the abil­ ity to distinguish human fat and muscle, BRI, WWI, and other indicators have been created. Therefore, their pre­ dictive ability and clinical application potential are signif­ icantly better than RFM, an indicator of BRI and WWI, which has certain advantages in promoting fat control and protecting the sleep health of obese people. The presence of interactions Population-wide subgroup analyses showed that the asso­ ciation between RFM and OSA was stronger in Mexican Americans, non-Hispanic blacks, mild physical activity and less crowd, people younger than 60, and women. In terms of race, a US study conducted between 1990 and 1994 showed that the incidence of OSA among eth­ nic minorities was as high as 16.3%, compared with 4.9% among non-Hispanic whites [48]. It has been demon­ strated that non-Hispanic blacks have a higher preva­ lence of OSA than other populations [49, 50]. This may be due to the higher probability of daytime sleepiness and snoring among non-Hispanic blacks [51], and both daytime sleepiness and snoring are among the evaluation criteria for OSA. In terms of physical activity, people with light physical activity or less have a higher risk of developing OSA, fol­ lowed by those with moderate physical activity and heavy physical activity. The risk of developing OSA seems to be negatively correlated with the intensity of physical activ­ ity. This result is the same as that of published experi­ ments, which also show that the intensity of physical activity is negatively correlated with OSA [52] and sleep disorders [53]. Regarding age, Pan et al. ‘s findings in the study of the correlation between BRI and OSA confirmed this result [22], and Zhang et al.‘s study of the correlation between Guo et al. Nutrition Journal (2025) 24:141 WWI and OSA also found this phenomenon [23]. The reason for this phenomenon may be that age affects the self-report of sleep and the difference in visceral fat and subcutaneous fat in the elderly compared with those under 60 years old. It has been confirmed that the selfreported snoring of the elderly decreases significantly after middle age [54, 55]. Snoring is one of the important markers for our evaluation of OSA, which may lead to a weaker correlation between RFM and OSA in people over 60 years old than in those under 60 years old. The reason for this result may be that age-related hearing loss affects the self-report of snoring in the elderly [14]. In addition, with the change of age, the visceral fat volume and subcutaneous fat distribution of the elderly and peo­ ple under 60 years old are also different [56], and fat dis­ tribution has an impact on the occurrence of OSA [40], which also suggests that we should pay more attention to obesity in young people. In terms of gender, the correlation between RFM and OSA in the female population is greater than that in the male population. This may be because menopausal hor­ monal changes lead to an increase in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) in women, thus making them more prone to OSA [57]. In addition, RFM is an index to evaluate obe­ sity, and its calculation formula includes waist circumfer­ ence, which has a good discrimination ability for central obesity. The increase of body weight and waist circum­ ference and the increase of the degree of central obesity in women after menopause [58, 59] may also increase the RFM index, thus affecting the correlation with OSA. Interaction effects of marital status on the association between RFM and OSA were also observed. The inter­ action of marital status may be due to the differences in stress among people with different marital statuses. Mar­ ried people have different levels of the stress hormone cortisol than unmarried and divorced people [60], and stress is associated with OSA and sleep disorders [61], which may lead to the difference in the incidence of OSA between cohabites and people living alone. In addition, compared with participants who were never married, those who were married or lived with a partner were more likely to have OSA than those in people living alone may also be related to the occurrence of OSA reported by partners mentioned by Young [14]. Compared with those living alone, the partners of cohabiting people can bet­ ter observe the occurrence of mild OSA and inform the participants, thus affecting the content of self-reports. Moreover, studies have confirmed that married people are more likely to be obese, and the probability of obe­ sity in married people is 88% higher than that in single, divorced, and widowed people [62]. Therefore, cohabit­ ing people are more likely to be obese, and RFM is one of the indicators of obesity. This clustering of obesity related to marriage may amplify the strength of the association between RFM and OSA. Therefore, marital status is an important moderator of the association between RFM and OSA by integrating social, behavioral, and biological factors. Mediating effect of hypertension Under the fully adjusted model, RFM was significantly associated with hypertension, and hypertension was significantly associated with OSA. According to the results of mediation analysis, hypertension may poten­ tially mediate the association between RFM and OSA. The reasons for this potentially mediating effect may be as follows: first, RFM is an indicator of obesity, and obe­ sity, especially visceral obesity, has been confirmed to be a promoting factor of hypertension [32–34]. Factors such as sympathetic nerve activation [63], endothelin, and oxidative stress [32] caused by obesity can promote the generation of hypertension. Secondly, Floras men­ tioned in the article that hypertension and OSA have a bidirectional and coexisting relationship [36], and a study confirmed that more than half of resistant hypertension patients have OSA [64], and OSA is also a promoting fac­ tor for hypertension and resistant hypertension [37]. In addition, there is excessive body fluid in patients with hypertension, which can cause body fluid of the limbs to move to the neck during redistribution at night, result­ ing in pharyngeal obstruction and further affecting OSA [36]. Because people with higher RFM index have more severe obesity, obese people are more likely to suffer from hypertension, and hypertension will further mediate the occurrence of OSA, so hypertension plays a mediating role in the correlation between RFM and OSA. However, it is undeniable that sensitivity analysis revealed that the mediating role of hypertension in the association between RFM and OSA was not robust, which may be attributed to the limitations of the study population, insufficiently adjusted covariates, and unknown confounding factors. However, we still believe that this potential mediating effect still has value, which can provide some clues or identify some errors in future research on hypertension, RFM, and OSA. Advantages and limitations of the study Our study has several design strengths that add cred­ ibility and precision to our experiments. For example, the complex weighting of NHANES data ensures diver­ sity and representativeness to reflect the characteristics of the U.S. population, and the same strict adherence to database protocols and guidelines increases accuracy and reduces bias. In this study, we used a multivariate logis­ tic regression model and reviewed the literature to screen and adjust many covariates related to RFM and OSA, which ensured that the regression model could better Guo et al. Nutrition Journal (2025) 24:141 reflect the association between RFM and OSA. In addi­ tion, subgroup analyses were performed to investigate the association between RFM and OSA and the interac­ tion of other factors on the association in different sub­ groups. Finally, we conducted a mediation analysis to investigate the potential role of hypertension in the posi­ tive relationship between RFM and OSA, and found the mediating role of hypertension. This study provides some epidemiological evidence for the prevention of OSA, which can provide new ideas for public health strategies to reduce the incidence of OSA. However, it has to be admitted that there are several shortcomings in our study, which need to be paid atten­ tion to and addressed in subsequent studies: (1) some of the use data are old, and the data collection period is inconsistent. Data on the frequency of snoring during sleep and the frequency of difficulty breathing, gasping, or stopping breathing during sleep were available in the NHANES database only from 2005 to 2008 and from 2015 to 2018. (2) This is a cross-sectional study, and the causal relationship between RFM and OSA cannot be established. The direction of causality among RFM, OSA, and hypertension remains unclear. The observed associa­ tions may be bidirectional or influenced by unmeasured confounders. More cohort studies are needed to inves­ tigate the temporal association between RFM and OSA and to evaluate the effect of reducing the RFM index on improving the prevalence of OSA. (3) OSA is a complex disease influenced by both genetic and environmental factors, and there may be confounding factors that are not captured in the NHANES database, so although we adjusted covariates as detailed as possible to reduce bias, there must still be incompleteness. Unknown confound­ ing factors that were not included in the study may have obscured or exaggerated the association between RFM and OSA, and the potential mediating role of hyperten­ sion between them. (4) Our assessment of OSA is sub­ jective and may be subject to recall bias and participants’ over- or under-reporting of symptoms, which may lead to inaccurate data. Although data from the NHANES sleep module have been validated and edited, milder OSA or snoring may not have been detected by participants, so people with OSA may have been missed in their assess­ ment. But, we still cannot deny the value of self-report in public health research because of its convenience and cost. However, OSA without evaluation by polysomnog­ raphy is inaccurate; we recommend further validation with the use of polysomnography in different popula­ tions and databases in future studies. (5) Although the potential mediating effect of hypertension on the associa­ tion between RFM and OSA was statistically significant across the current study population and covariates, its robustness was weak, and it is easily affected by unknown confounding factors. So, we hope that more prospective studies with adequate adjustment for unknown con­ founders to confirm or rule out the mediating effect of hypertension and improve the robustness of its mediat­ ing effect. Conclusion The current study has proved that there is a positive and nonlinear correlation between RFM and OSA. This asso­ ciation was more pronounced among Mexican Ameri­ cans, non-Hispanic blacks, mild physical activity and less crowd, people under 60 years of age, and women. Hypertension plays a potential mediating role in the posi­ tive association between RFM and OSA, but its robust­ ness is poor and vulnerable to interference by unknown confounding factors. RFM shows potential as a predictor of OSA, but more prospective studies are needed to con­ firm these findings and determine the causal relationship between RFM and OSA, and to verify whether a potential mediating effect of hypertension exists. However, the relationship between TyG index and OSA has not been adequately assessed. This study aimed to evaluate the association between TyG index and OSA. Methods: TyG index was assessed in 180 (mean age: 48.6 ± 13.8 years; 73.9% male) consecutive Korean adults with suspected OSA admitted to the sleep clinic at St. Paul’s Hospital between 2010 and 2012. The occurrence of more than 5 apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) events/h was used to define OSA. TyG index was calculated using the following equation: In [fasting triglycerides (mg/dL) × fasting glucose (mg/dL)/2]. All participants were grouped according to TyG index tertiles. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was used to determine factors associated with increased OSA risk. Results: The overall prevalence of OSA in study participants was determined to be 83.9%. The prevalence of OSA increased (I [lowest]: 71.6%; II: 88.7%; III [highest]: 91.4%), and lowest peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) levels decreased (I: 83.3 ± 8.5%; II: 79.9 ± 8.7%; III: 79.0 ± 8.3%), as TyG index tertile increased (P < 0.05). TyG index was correlated with AHI (r = 0.179) and lowest SpO2 (r = −0.188) (P < 0.05, respectively). Univariate linear regression analysis revealed an association between TyG and AHI (β = 10.084; P = 0.016). Multivariate logistic regression analysis showed that TyG index (odds ratio [OR]: 3.348; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.081–10.372), age ≥55 years (OR: 5.426; 95% CI: 1.642–17.935), and obesity (OR: 3.801; 95% CI: 1.468–9.842) were associated with increased OSA risk (all P < 0.05). The optimal TyG index cut-off value for predicting OSA was 8.83 (sensitivity: 61.6%; specificity: 69.0%; area under the curve: 0.688; P = 0.001). The predictive value of the OSA cut-off value improved when age ≥55 years and obesity were considered. Conclusion: Increased TyG index was independently associated with increased OSA risk.
